title: 7. Why the Price Is What It Is: Valuation, Reverse DCF & Peer Comps
web_title: 7. Why the Price Is What It Is: Valuation, Reverse DCF & Peer Comps
book_title: 7. Why the Price Is What It Is: Valuation, Reverse DCF & Peer Comps
question: At ₹2,105.60 on the 23 November NSE ledger and ₹2,054.80 on the 25 November live TradingView close, what future cash-flow growth and terminal durability is the market pricing in, and how do our Pass 1 blind spots reshape fair value?

epigraph.quote: Price is what you pay; value is what you get.
epigraph.author: Benjamin Graham, as quoted by Warren Buffett in the 2008 Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letter

web_blocks.html: Chapters 1 to 6 judged the business without looking at a share quote. Now we put a price on it. Two distinct market prints govern this refresh, and we keep them strictly separate throughout. The verified NSE ledger close for 23 November 2026 is ₹2,105.60 [90]. Two sessions later, the live TradingView snapshot for 25 November 2026 shows a close of ₹2,054.80 (−2.41% on the day) [91]. Both sit well below the prior monograph close of ₹2,297.00 on 12 November 2026. The diluted share count remains 17,105,816 (1.7106 Cr), unchanged since the FY22 buyback [1]. Market capitalisation is therefore ₹3,601.8 Cr at the 23 November ledger close and ₹3,514.9 Cr at the 25 November live print (Screener rounds this to ₹3,515 Cr; TradingView displays ₹3,601.54 Cr using a slightly higher share base) [91, 93]. Cash stood at ₹163.23 Cr on 30 September 2026 with zero bank debt after the Unbound Medicine loan was repaid in August [2, 106]. Adding roughly ₹18 Cr of lease liabilities places enterprise value at ₹3,456.6 Cr on the 23 November ledger and ₹3,369.7 Cr on the 25 November live close.
The valuation dashboard immediately below compares every headline multiple across both session dates so readers can see how the two-day break below ₹2,085 compressed trailing and forward multiples.

web_blocks.takeaway: On headline numbers, MPS looks optically cheaper than two weeks ago: 18.86x trailing earnings on TradingView, 16.7x refreshed FY27E earnings, and 10.8x forward EBITDA at the 25 November close of ₹2,054.80. A 6.3% forward cash-flow yield on a debt-free 35% to 39% ROCE business always catches the eye. Yet optical cheapness is never a buy signal by itself. Our Pass 1 refresh uncovered organic Education contraction, Unbound's royalty-capped margin and OpenEvidence rivalry, and a sharp Research hiring surge that explain why the market is still repricing terminal durability.

Each fiscal year's audited earnings per share enters the denominator from 1 June following year-end, so the band captures true historical investor moods across bull runs and drawdowns.

web_blocks.takeaway: Even after sliding 31% off its August 52-week high, MPS at 20.3x FY26 EPS (25 November live print) and 20.8x (23 November ledger) still trades above its ten-year median of 17.6x. It has fallen below the five-year median of 22.7x, but it is nowhere near the 13.8x to 16.0x trough multiples seen during prior deratings. Multiple compression can travel further whenever growth doubts appear.

web_blocks.takeaway: Three drawdowns exceeding 50% since 2015 (−57.7%, −67.5%, and −51.9%) establish the true volatility base rate of this stock. In 2025 to 2026, trailing EPS grew from ₹69.43 to ₹87.05 and then ₹101.26, yet the multiple collapsed from 41.7x to 16.0x. The multiple, not next quarter's earnings, drives most of the drawdown risk.

web_blocks.takeaway: MPS is no longer escaping the sector AI derating. Over three months to 25 November 2026, MPS fell 24.6%—matching eClerx (−24.5%) and trailing Newgen (−21.2%). Worse, the October 2026 Johns Hopkins collaboration with free clinical-AI leader OpenEvidence introduced a company-specific terminal-value threat to Unbound Medicine that was missing from our November 12 underwriting.

web_blocks.title: NARRATOR'S NOTE: a multiple is a mood about terminal value, not next quarter's EBITDA
paragraphs: When MPS raises its FY27 EBITDA floor to at least ₹310 Cr on 4 November and the stock still drops 11% over the next three weeks, the market is telling you something specific. Investors are not disputing H1 FY27's ₹154 Cr of banked EBITDA. They are questioning how much margin survives 2028 to 2032 once AI reprices production rates and free clinical AI challenges licensed reference apps.

Our response is disciplined arithmetic. First, solve for the free-cash-flow growth embedded in today's price via a reverse discounted cash flow. Second, test whether our newly audited Pass 1 facts make that implied growth easy or fragile.

web_blocks.html: We run a ten-year reverse discounted cash flow anchored on refreshed FY27E Base free cash flow to the firm of ₹212.0 Cr. That starting figure builds from ₹312 Cr EBITDA, less ₹36 Cr depreciation, less 25% tax on EBIT, plus ₹36 Cr depreciation, less ₹11 Cr capital expenditure, ₹5 Cr lease outflows, and a ₹15 Cr working-capital build. That equals a 6.1% yield on the 23 November enterprise value of ₹3,456.6 Cr and a 6.3% yield on the 25 November live enterprise value of ₹3,369.7 Cr. Free-cash-flow growth fades linearly over ten years from the solved year-one rate to the terminal rate.

web_blocks.the_number: At the 23 November ledger close of ₹2,105.60 (EV ₹3,457 Cr), a 13% hurdle rate and 5% terminal growth require 10.5% year-one free-cash-flow growth fading linearly to 5% (7.8% average over ten years). At the 25 November live close of ₹2,054.80 (EV ₹3,370 Cr), the requirement falls to 9.9% in year one (7.4% average).
web_blocks.how_calculated: Set enterprise value equal to the present value of ten years of free cash flow to the firm plus a Gordon-growth terminal value, then solve numerically for the year-one growth rate under linear fade to terminal growth.
web_blocks.the_inputs: Base FY27E FCFF of ₹212.0 Cr (EBITDA ₹312 Cr, D&A ₹36 Cr, tax 25% on EBIT, capex ₹11 Cr, leases ₹5 Cr, working-capital build ₹15 Cr), discount rate 13%, terminal growth 5%, and verified ledger EV ₹3,456.6 Cr (live TV EV ₹3,369.7 Cr).
web_blocks.the_range: At 12% and 5% terminal growth, ledger EV needs just 7.1% year-one growth. At 14% and 5%, it needs 13.7%. At 13% and 4%, it needs 12.9%. Across the full 11% to 15% discount-rate and 3% to 6% terminal-growth grid, required year-one growth spans −0.2% to 20.6%.
web_blocks.if_off: If free cash flow compounds at a steady 8.0% for ten years and 5% thereafter, a buyer earns 13.0% a year from ₹2,105.60 and 13.2% from ₹2,054.80. If AI price give-back and Education erosion hold growth to 5.0%, the return slips to 11.4% to 11.6%—below our 13% small-cap hurdle.

web_blocks.html: The sensitivity grid lays out the exact year-one free-cash-flow growth required across twenty combinations of discount rates and terminal growth rates at the verified 23 November ledger enterprise value of ₹3,457 Cr.

web_blocks.caption: Reverse DCF grid: implied year-one FCFF growth (%), fading linearly to terminal growth over ten years, at 23 November ledger EV ₹3,457 Cr and FY27E FCFF ₹212.0 Cr
web_blocks.takeaway: Inside the realistic small-cap band of 12% to 14% hurdle rates and 4% to 5% terminal growth, the market requires 7.1% to 15.9% year-one free-cash-flow growth. The central cell (13% / 5%) asks for 10.5% in year one (9.9% at the 25 November live print)—almost identical to MPS's 10.2% eleven-year EBITDA CAGR. Bears sit in the 14% to 15% / 3% corner (17.9% to 20.6%), pricing weak terminal longevity.

web_blocks.html: Inverting the model shows the annualised equity return a long-term buyer earns across five constant ten-year free-cash-flow growth rates at both the 23 November ledger close and the 25 November live print.

web_blocks.caption: Implied 10-year annual return at constant FCF growth (5% terminal rate; starting FY27E FCFF ₹212.0 Cr)
headers: Implied IRR at 25 Nov live TV (₹2,054.80)
web_blocks.takeaway: On an acquisition-free cash-flow base (₹212.0 Cr FCFF), repeating MPS's 10.2% eleven-year EBITDA CAGR implies a 14.2% to 14.4% annual return. However, that baseline credits acquisition-fueled historical growth without deducting historical acquisition spend. Charging M&A reinvestment below cuts the implied return under our 13% hurdle.

web_blocks.html: M&A-Adjusted Owner FCFF Stress Audit (Red-Team Reinvestment Check). MPS's historical 10.2% eleven-year EBITDA CAGR and 12.7%/17.1% five-year CAGRs were not free organic growth. Per Chapter 1, four priced FY22–FY26 deals—EI Design (₹42.09 Cr), Liberate (₹70.33 Cr), AJE (₹69.67 Cr), and Unbound Medicine (₹140.40 Cr)—consumed ₹322.49 Cr (₹64.5 Cr per year), with AJE supplying ~92% of FY25 sales growth and Unbound supplying over 100% of H1 FY27 Education growth [1, 15, 102]. Separately, FY23–FY26 working-capital drag averaged ₹24 Cr per year (Chapter 6) against ₹15 Cr in our base FCFF. Deducting ₹64.5 Cr/yr of acquisition reinvestment lowers owner FCFF to ₹147.5 Cr (and ₹138.5 Cr if working capital normalizes to ₹24 Cr).

web_blocks.caption: M&A-Adjusted Owner FCFF Reverse DCF & Red-Team Stress Audit (13% hurdle, 5% terminal growth; 23 Nov ledger EV ₹3,456.6 Cr / 25 Nov live TV EV ₹3,369.7 Cr)
headers: Required Y1 growth (13% / 5%) — ledger / live TV
Implied IRR at 10.2% 10Y growth — ledger / live TV
rows: Acquisition-free Base FCFF (zero M&A, ₹15 Cr WC)
Clears 13% hurdle only if 10.2% growth is achieved organically without deal spend
M&A-Adjusted Owner FCFF (−₹64.5 Cr/yr avg FY22–FY26 deals)
Fails 13% hurdle (−130 to −140 bps); required Y1 growth nearly doubles

web_blocks.takeaway: Once we stop treating acquisition-fueled growth as free, the long-term cash-flow case drops below our 13% small-cap hurdle. Deducting ₹64.5 Cr/yr of historical M&A reinvestment cuts owner FCFF to ₹147.5 Cr, lifts required Year-1 growth to 20.0% (ledger) / 19.3% (live TV), and compresses the 10.2%-growth IRR to 11.6%–11.7% (11.2%–11.4% at ₹24 Cr working-capital drag)—directly reinforcing our REJECTED verdict.

web_blocks.html: Why does the market refuse to pay more than 18.86x trailing earnings for a 38.7% ROCE franchise? Our Pass 1 blind-spot audit surfaced four concrete fundamental overhangs that sharpen the skepticism beyond generic AI fear. First, organic Education is contracting and Unbound is royalty-capped. Subtracting Unbound Medicine's disclosed Q2 revenue of ₹21.07 Cr and EBITDA of ₹3.82 Cr (18.13% margin; H1 ₹41.64 Cr revenue / ₹7.48 Cr EBITDA = 17.96%) from Education Solutions reveals that organic Education contracted −3.8% YoY in H1 and −9.9% YoY in Q2, while organic Q2 EBITDA fell −23.3% YoY (₹17.07 Cr vs ₹22.25 Cr) [102, 104]. Management's own Q2 presentation confirms Unbound's royalty-based third-party content model carries a structurally lower margin ceiling than MPS's solutions base [102]. Second, OpenEvidence directly threatens Unbound's moat. A Harvard Medical School study in JAMA (15 October 2026) showed OpenEvidence reaching 703,265 monthly active U.S. clinicians for free, and on 13 October 2026 Johns Hopkins Medicine—one of Unbound's flagship licensors—signed a landmark AI medical-education alliance with OpenEvidence while Wolters Kluwer's UpToDate Expert AI reached 2,500 U.S. hospitals [99, 100, 101]. Third, Research headcount jumped ahead of billing. Group headcount rose +11.16% YoY to 3,557 in Q2 FY27, driven by Research Solutions headcount surging +18.02% YoY to 2,666 (+20.42% ex-AJE)—nearly matching +21.71% ex-AJE revenue growth [103]. Until November–December mandate billing converts, the near-flat headcount AI-leverage story is unproven. Fourth, governance and concentration remain real discounts: one customer is 17.3% of revenue, goodwill plus acquired intangibles are 52.5% of assets, the Chief People Officer resigned inside four months amid 28.85% attrition, and merchant banker D&A Financial Services disclaimed independent financial, legal, or tax due diligence on the ADI BPO promoter merger despite pending tax proceedings [1, 107, 108].

Next we benchmark MPS against four listed Indian knowledge-process, BPM, and software peers pulled from the same 25 November 2026 live TradingView snapshot: eClerx Services (data and knowledge workflows), Firstsource Solutions (BPM), Newgen Software (content and process platforms), and Cyient (ER&D and digital engineering). For full session transparency, 23 November 2026 verified NSE ledger closes were ₹2,105.60 for MPS, ₹1,511.40 for eClerx, ₹283.60 for Firstsource, and ₹1,160.50 for Cyient (Newgen is priced from the 25 November live snapshot).

web_blocks.caption: MPS and listed Indian peers: valuation, profitability, growth, and Weinstein stage (25 November 2026 live TradingView snapshot)
web_blocks.takeaway: MPS leads every listed peer in operating margin (29.4% TTM in the table above; 29.45% unrounded on TradingView vs 9.5% to 23.7%), return on equity (31.0% vs 7.0% to 26.2%), and return on capital employed (38.7% Screener vs 12.3% to 34.4%), while carrying virtually zero debt (0.03x D/E). Yet MPS trades at 18.9x TTM P/E—practically on top of Stage 4 peers eClerx (19.1x, down 34.9% over 1Y) and Newgen (18.5x, down 53.5% over 1Y), and far below Stage 2 peers Firstsource (28.1x) and Cyient (33.8x). The market is grouping MPS with high-margin content and KPO vendors facing AI-deflation fear rather than awarding a Stage 2 rerating. Note that TradingView's ₹3,601.54 Cr market cap for MPS uses a wider share count than our verified 1.7106 Cr shares (₹3,514.9 Cr at ₹2,054.80).

web_blocks.takeaway: MPS spans both halves of the AI ledger. Its core Research workflow and journal platforms earn near-50% margins like an embedded software toll-booth, yet its production book faces RWS-style unit-rate pressure and Unbound now confronts both Wolters Kluwer's 2,500-hospital scale and free OpenEvidence at Johns Hopkins. That split prevents us from paying an unqualified software multiple.

web_blocks.html: We now re-underwrite our 12-month scenario values (value date November 2027) from first principles to reflect every Pass 1 finding. Compared with our 12 November monograph, we trim Base FY27E EBITDA from ₹315 Cr to ₹312 Cr (still above the CFO's ₹310 Cr floor), lower Base FY28E EBITDA from ₹360 Cr to ₹345 Cr (+10.6% YoY, reflecting Unbound's ~18% royalty cap and cautious organic Education recovery), shift Bear probability from 25% to 30% (Bull trimmed to 20%), and tighten Base and Bull exit multiples to 17.5x (ten-year median 17.6x) and 21.0x (below the five-year median 22.7x). All scenarios keep D&A at ₹36 Cr (FY27E) and ₹38 Cr (FY28E), other income ₹8 Cr, interest ₹3 Cr, tax 25%, and 1.7106 Cr shares. As before, we report both Basis B (central LTM EPS at the value date, averaging FY27E and FY28E) and Basis A (stricter year-end FY27E EPS matching the historical band).

web_blocks.caption: Refreshed Basis B (central case): probability-weighted 12-month valuation on LTM EPS at November 2027 (compared against both 23 Nov ledger ₹2,105.60 and 25 Nov live TV ₹2,054.80)
web_blocks.takeaway: Even after the drop to ₹2,105.60 (23 Nov ledger) and ₹2,054.80 (25 Nov live TV), the refreshed probability-weighted value of ₹2,231 offers only +6.0% to +8.6% expected 12-month upside—well short of a 13% Indian small-cap hurdle. Our Base value of ₹2,275 sits just +8.0% above the ledger close and +10.7% above live TV, while Bear risk to ₹1,593 exposes −22.5% to −24.4% downside.

web_blocks.html: Putting both earnings bases side by side confirms that the conclusion holds even without relying on FY28E growth. On stricter year-end earnings (Basis A), expected return is nearly flat.

web_blocks.caption: Two earnings bases for the refreshed scenarios: Basis A (strict FY27E year-end EPS) and Basis B (central LTM EPS at November 2027)

web_blocks.takeaway: On Basis A—which matches how our ten-year P/E band is constructed—the probability-weighted value is ₹2,117, leaving just +0.5% upside from the 23 November ledger close and +3.0% from the 25 November live print. Even on central Basis B, +6.0% to +8.6% expected return does not compensate for buying into a confirmed Stage 4 downtrend.

web_blocks.takeaway: Because H1 FY27 already banked ₹154 Cr of EBITDA, our central Bear case (₹1,593 at 14.0x) leaves November 2027 LTM EPS 12.4% above FY26. However, that central Bear stops at the 25th-percentile multiple and keeps FY28E EBITDA at ₹285 Cr. The Severe-Bear stress test below explicitly models an RWS-style margin reset and Wolters Kluwer-style 12.5x multiple trough.

web_blocks.html: Severe-Bear / RWS-Style Stress Test (Red-Team Downside Audit). What if H2 FY27 Research billing fails to offset Q2's +20.42% ex-AJE hiring surge while organic Education remains negative—pulling FY27E EBITDA below the ₹310 Cr floor to ₹295.0 Cr (PAT ₹198.0 Cr, EPS ₹115.75)? And what if FY28E revenue stalls near annualized H1 (₹900 Cr) while AI renewal give-back and Unbound attrition compress consolidated EBITDA margin to 28.5% (just below FY25's 29.0% strong-form bear line from Chapter 4, echoing RWS Holdings' 600 bps reset) to yield ₹256.5 Cr EBITDA (PAT ₹167.6 Cr, EPS ₹97.99; Nov 2027 LTM EPS ₹106.87) [67]? Applying 12.5x—between MPS's 10th-percentile multiple (11.7x; Feb 2019 trough 11.5x) and Wolters Kluwer's 2026 buyback multiple (12.8x)—cuts Bear value to ₹1,336, matching MPS's March 2026 intraday low (₹1,336.10) [65, 89, 90].

web_blocks.takeaway: Replacing our central ₹1,593 Bear with the ₹1,336 Severe-Bear stress case (0.30 × ₹1,336 + 0.50 × ₹2,275 + 0.20 × ₹3,080 = ₹2,154 on Basis B; Basis A Bear ₹115.75 × 12.5 = ₹1,447 -> ₹2,059) cuts Basis B weighted upside to just +2.3% (ledger) / +4.8% (live TV) and Basis A to −2.2% / +0.2%. Both central and stressed downside math independently reinforce our REJECTED (0% allocation) verdict.

web_blocks.the_number: Refreshed Base-case LTM EPS (Basis B) at November 2027 is ₹130.0 (average of FY27E ₹123.2 and FY28E ₹136.8). Applied at the ten-year median multiple of 17.5x, Base fair value is ₹2,275 per share.
web_blocks.how_calculated: Subtract ₹36 Cr D&A (FY27E) and ₹38 Cr D&A (FY28E) from Base EBITDA of ₹312 Cr and ₹345 Cr, add ₹8 Cr other income, deduct ₹3 Cr interest, apply a 25% tax rate, and divide by 1.7106 Cr shares.
web_blocks.the_inputs: FY27E EBITDA ₹312 Cr (above CFO Prarthana Agarwal's ₹310 Cr floor), FY28E EBITDA ₹345 Cr (+10.6% organic compounding with no assumed deal), 25% tax rate matching H1 FY27, and unchanged 1.7106 Cr shares.
web_blocks.the_range: Central Bear LTM EPS is ₹113.8 (₹1,593 at 14.0x), Severe-Bear LTM EPS is ₹106.87 (₹1,336 at 12.5x), and Bull LTM EPS is ₹146.7 (₹3,080 at 21.0x). Every ₹10 Cr swing in both years' EBITDA shifts LTM EPS by ₹4.38 (₹77 per share at 17.5x). Each single turn of P/E moves Base value by ₹130 per share (6.3% of the 25 November live price).
web_blocks.if_off: Multiple sensitivity outweighs near-term EBITDA sensitivity. If Research billing conversion stalls in H2 FY27 and Education keeps shrinking, a 14.0x multiple on ₹113.8 EPS pulls the stock toward ₹1,593—and an RWS-style margin reset below 29% at 12.5x opens ₹1,336 (−35.0% to −36.6%). Conversely, proving organic Education recovery and 47%+ Research margins would justify lifting Base fair value back toward ₹2,500+.

web_blocks.company: Wolters Kluwer (information, software and clinical-reference platforms)
web_blocks.region_era: Netherlands, global; February to November 2026 AI-disruption derating
web_blocks.mechanism: A high-ROCE information franchise with 83% recurring revenue suffered a 47% average-price compression after Anthropic released its Claude legal plug-in on 3 February 2026 [65, 85]. Morningstar lowered Wolters Kluwer from wide moat to narrow moat on 5 March 2026 even though reported revenue and profit growth never slowed [85].
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: FY25 organic revenue grew 6% to €6,125m at a 27.5% adjusted operating margin, diluted adjusted EPS rose 9% to €5.29, and 9M 2026 organic growth held at 6% with 10% operating-profit growth [65, 89]. Yet average share-buyback prices fell from €128.45 in 2025 (~24.3x) to €67.97 through 3 November 2026 (~12.8x)—a 47% derating while earnings rose [65, 89].
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: Quality earnings alone cannot arrest a terminal-value multiple reset. If Wolters Kluwer—with 83% recurring revenue and UpToDate Expert AI across 2,500 U.S. hospitals—compressed to ~13x earnings, MPS (with ~45% recurring revenue and Unbound now facing OpenEvidence at Johns Hopkins) cannot rely on valuation optics to put in a floor while its chart is breaking down.

web_blocks.html: Valuation upgrade and downgrade triggers. We lift fair value back above ₹2,400 only when four fundamental proofs arrive together: H2 FY27 EBITDA delivers at least ₹156 Cr (securing the ₹310 Cr floor), Research Solutions holds at least a 45% margin as November–December mandate billing scales revenue per employee, organic Education ex-Unbound returns to positive YoY revenue growth in H2 FY27, and Unbound Medicine proves institutional renewal resilience at or above 90% despite OpenEvidence. Conversely, we shift probability directly into the ₹1,593 Bear / ₹1,336 Severe-Bear band if Research margin slips below 42% for two quarters, organic Education stays negative through FY27, FY27 EBITDA guidance drops below ₹300 Cr, a goodwill write-down exceeds ₹25 Cr, or final ADI BPO sanction reveals adverse tax liabilities or public dilution.

Valuation therefore delivers a clear bridge to Chapter 8. At ₹2,105.60 (23 November ledger) and ₹2,054.80 (25 November live TradingView close), MPS is modestly cheaper than two weeks ago, yet our refreshed Pass 1 adjustments leave probability-weighted upside at just +6.0% to +8.6% (+2.3% to +4.8% under Severe-Bear ₹1,336 stress; +0.5% to +3.0% on strict year-end earnings) and cut M&A-adjusted ten-year IRR below our 13% hurdle to 11.6%–11.7%. There is no deep margin of safety to override a broken trend. Chapter 8 examines why the tape has now crossed decisively into Stage 4 and why catching a falling knife here violates our core risk discipline.

book_paragraphs: After six chapters of auditing the business without looking at the quote, we open the price screen and find a tempting optical trap. On the verified 23 November 2026 NSE ledger, MPS closed at ₹2,105.60. Two sessions later, on the 25 November live TradingView tape, it closed at ₹2,054.80—down 31 per cent from its August high of ₹2,979. At ₹2,055 the company is valued at roughly ₹3,515 crore, or ₹3,370 crore after subtracting its ₹163 crore of cash and adding modest lease obligations. That works out to about 19 times trailing earnings, 17 times our refreshed FY27 estimate, and under 11 times forward EBITDA. For a debt-free business earning 35 to 39 per cent on capital, a first glance whispers bargain.

Resist that whisper. Valuation is never a single number; it is a comparison between what the price asks for and what the freshly audited business can safely deliver. Over the past decade MPS has traded between 4.7 times and 41.7 times last-reported annual earnings, with a ten-year median of 17.6 times and a five-year median of 22.7 times. Today's 20.3 times FY26 profit sits below the recent five-year average, yet still fifteen per cent richer than the ten-year norm. More importantly, this stock has suffered three drawdowns exceeding fifty per cent since 2015—including a 52 per cent collapse from March 2025 to March 2026 while earnings per share actually climbed sixteen per cent. In MPS, the multiple does the violence long before reported profit stumbles.

Our reverse discounted cash flow exposes an even sharper catch once you stop treating acquisition-fueled growth as free. On an acquisition-free ₹212 crore base FY27 free cash flow, today's enterprise value asks for 10.5 per cent year-one growth on the ledger (9.9 per cent live) at a 13 per cent hurdle—making MPS's 10.2 per cent eleven-year EBITDA CAGR look like a 14.2 to 14.4 per cent return. Yet four priced FY22–FY26 deals alone cost ₹322.5 crore, or ₹64.5 crore per year. Deducting that ₹64.5 crore of annual M&A reinvestment lowers owner free cash flow to ₹147.5 crore, doubles required year-one growth to 20.0 per cent (ledger) / 19.3 per cent (live), and cuts the 10.2 per cent growth return to 11.6–11.7 per cent (11.2–11.4 per cent if working-capital drag normalizes to ₹24 crore)—below our 13 per cent small-cap hurdle.

And that is exactly where our Pass 1 refresh changed the valuation equation. Between November 12 and November 25, digging into the BSE-filed Q2 presentation and October–November industry disclosures uncovered four real bruises. First, once you strip out acquired Unbound Medicine—which runs on a royalty-bearing third-party licensing model capped near 18 per cent EBITDA margin—organic Education revenue actually shrank almost ten per cent in Q2, and organic Education EBITDA fell 23 per cent. Second, OpenEvidence surged to more than 703,000 monthly active American clinicians for free and signed a flagship AI medical-education alliance directly with Johns Hopkins Medicine, one of Unbound's own marquee licensors. Third, Research Solutions headcount jumped over 20 per cent outside AJE to staff upcoming mandates, putting the near-flat headcount AI leverage thesis on probation until second-half billing shows up. Fourth, direct publishing rivals Lumina Datamatics—now owning 100 per cent of TNQTech—and Straive are launching competing AI platforms, while the ADI BPO promoter merger carries a merchant-banker due-diligence disclaimer alongside pending tax cases.

Putting those facts into a fresh twelve-month valuation trims our numbers honestly. On central last-twelve-months earnings of ₹130 per share at November 2027, our Base value is ₹2,275 at 17.5 times, central Bear is ₹1,593 at 14 times (30 per cent weight), and Bull is ₹3,080 at 21 times (20 per cent weight)—giving a weighted value of ₹2,231 (+6.0 per cent ledger / +8.6 per cent live; ₹2,117 on stricter FY27 earnings). Stress-testing further for an RWS-style margin reset to 28.5 per cent on flat ₹900 crore FY28 sales (₹256.5 crore EBITDA, ₹106.87 LTM EPS) at a Wolters Kluwer-style 12.5 times multiple opens Severe-Bear downside to ₹1,336 (−36.6 per cent ledger / −35.0 per cent live), cutting weighted upside to just +2.3 to +4.8 per cent (+0.2 per cent to −2.2 per cent on strict FY27 earnings).

When a business offers only two to nine per cent expected upside against 22 to 37 per cent Bear downside, delivers sub-12 per cent M&A-adjusted IRR, and sits inside a global sector derating where even Wolters Kluwer compressed nearly 50 per cent while growing profits, valuation does not justify overriding a broken chart. That brings us directly to the tape in Chapter 8.

book_callouts.title: Why 18.9x P/E is not a margin of safety yet
book_callouts.quote: Optical cheapness on trailing earnings is a trap when the market is repricing terminal value.
book_callouts.text: Our refreshed Bear, Base, and Bull scenarios incorporate organic Education contraction, Unbound's royalty cap and OpenEvidence threat, and Research pre-hiring. Even after a 31% drop from the August high, expected 12-month return is below our 13% cost of equity.
bullets: Refreshed Base value falls from ₹2,410 to ₹2,275 (17.5x central LTM EPS ₹130.0).
Probability-weighted value is ₹2,231 (+6.0% vs 23 Nov ledger ₹2,105.60; +8.6% vs 25 Nov live TV ₹2,054.80).
Bear case of ₹1,593 (30% weight, 14x) leaves −22.5% to −24.4% downside if AI give-back and Education softness persist.

book_subsections.title: What the Indian peer group and Wolters Kluwer tell us
paragraphs: Pulling the live 25 November peer screen confirms that MPS is not suffering in isolation. eClerx Services—another high-margin Indian knowledge-process leader with 34.4 per cent return on capital—sits in Stage 4 at 19.1 times earnings after falling 35 per cent over the past year. Newgen Software sits in Stage 4 at 18.5 times earnings, down 53 per cent over twelve months. Meanwhile Stage 2 IT and BPM peers such as Firstsource and Cyient command 28 to 34 times earnings despite generating less than half of MPS's margins and returns on capital.

That split is instructive. The market is paying up for companies whose trend and AI narrative have stabilized, while compressing multiples on content and knowledge-workflow names until contract renewals prove margins survive. Wolters Kluwer's 2026 journey reinforces the lesson: its operating profit grew ten per cent in constant currency during the first nine months of 2026, yet its average buyback price still slid from €128 to €68. When the whole neighborhood is repricing terminal durability, patience is not pessimism—it is capital preservation.
